_what_this_is: THE STRUCTURAL PIECE KIT. Six pieces. A player places these on the deck grid and a
deckhouse emerges from the placements; nobody ever types a corner coordinate and nobody
ever describes a room and has it materialise at a custom size.
THE SPLIT. `plate`, `spar`, `wire`, `sheer_band` are the BAKING layer - general geometry,
already proven, unchanged by this file. This is the AUTHORING layer: a piece is a named
thing with a footprint in CELLS that RESOLVES into those primitives. StructureBaker never
learns a new word.
THE RULE THAT MAKES THIS MINECRAFT AND NOT CAD, and every entry below obeys it:
EVERY PARAMETER TAKES ITS VALUE FROM A DECLARED FINITE SET, AND EVERY GEOMETRIC
PARAMETER IS COUNTED IN GRID UNITS.
Lengths and heights are whole CELLS (0.5 m). Rakes are whole QUARTER-CELLS (0.25 m).
Openings, gauges and profiles are named choices. No float is ever typed by a player, so
two pieces placed side by side meet exactly - which is the property a kit lives or dies on.
WHY RAKE IS A PARAMETER AND NOT A SET OF FIXED VARIANTS. Covering this repo's existing
vessels with fixed rakes needs 0, 3, 7, 11, 12, 17, 20 degrees - seven variants of every
wall piece, which is seven times the thing a player has to learn for one axis of variation.
Quantising the rake to a quarter-cell of top-edge offset gives the same guarantee a fixed
set was bought for (neighbours match, no slot of daylight opens between them) at the cost
of one number picked off a nine-entry list.
WHY THE CORNER IS ITS OWN PIECE, and this is the piece that beats blockiness. Two raked
walls meeting at 90 degrees do NOT meet: each top edge has moved outboard along its own
normal, so a wedge opens at the corner exactly as wide as the rake. `corner_45` is the
adapter. Its two vertical edges belong to its two neighbours and its single plate is
BILINEAR, so it absorbs any difference between the two rakes - including a raked front
meeting a plumb side, which is the trawler's whole forward end. The by-product is that a
raked house is chamfered at every corner by construction, and a chamfered corner is the
one thing a stack of square panels can never look like.
PLACEMENT. A piece is placed at a grid NODE (a corner between cells), not in a cell:
walls stand on cell edges. `cell` is [x, y, z] in whole cells; the piece-local frame has
+X along the run, +Y up and the OUTWARD face toward -Z; `facing` is 0/90/180/270 degrees
of yaw. Fittings - chairs, cleats, lanterns, seats - are NOT pieces and never snap: they
are `items[]` with float coordinates and PartCatalog owns them. Over half the 344 rows in
COMPONENTS.md are smaller than one cell.
WHAT THE KIT DELIBERATELY REFUSES. A sheer-following bulwark is a swept curve and belongs
to `edges[]`/sheer_band. Quantising it to the grid would step the one curve the whole fleet
was rebuilt to draw, so no piece here tries.

pieces.description: One plate of a deckhouse side, plumb or raked, optionally with a door, a window or a scuttle punched through it. The workhorse: everything that is not a corner, a window band, a deck or a trim run is this.

span._is: length of the run. Six standard widths, the way a merchant sells plate.

height._is: 1.0 m to 3.0 m. 5 cells = 2.5 m is a tier; 2 cells = 1.0 m is a bulwark or a coaming course.

rake._is: how far the TOP edge stands outboard of the foot, in 0.25 m steps. Positive rakes out (a trawler's front), negative tumbles home (a side). At the 2.5 m tier height this spans -21.8 to +21.8 degrees, which covers every rake in the fleet.

opening._is: a real hole with its proud casing, centred on the panel. A door is 0.85 x 1.95 m against a 1.8 m figure; a window 0.80 x 0.70 at 1.20 m sill; a scuttle 0.40 x 0.40. The opening is the piece, not a set of four numbers - which is why span is fixed by what fits, not by the hole.

pieces.description: A wheelhouse or saloon wall carrying a RIBBON WINDOW: a coaming course, a dark glass plate set 90 mm into the reveal, a header above it and mullions standing in the reveal. One piece, four to seven plates. A ribbon is not a row of holes - the ferry proved that the hard way - so it is a different piece from a punched window, not a parameter of one.

rake._is: the whole wall rakes, and the coaming, glass, header and mullions all lean with it - the band follows the wall rather than sitting on it.

sill._is: coaming height under the glass. 2 cells = 1.0 m, which is the fall-barrier dimension the 1.8 m figure sets.

lights._is: panes across the run. lights-1 mullions, evenly spaced, 0.10 m wide IN METRES - authored as a fraction of the plate they came out 3 m wide on a ferry and the band read as portholes.

constraints._is: sill 3 and band 3 in a 4-cell wall are two legal picks that leave no header, and a zero-height header is a degenerate quad. At least one cell of wall must stand above the glass.

pieces.description: THE PIECE THAT BEATS BLOCKINESS. A 45-degree chord across a corner of `span` cells, carrying the transition between the two walls that meet there. Its two vertical edges are those walls' end edges, so it closes the wedge that opens when a raked wall meets a wall raked differently - the plate is bilinear and a twisted quad is exactly what it is for. At span 1 it is a 0.71 m knuckle on a deckhouse corner; at span 3 it is a fast ferry's bow facet. Placed 180 degrees round it fills a concave corner instead, so there is no second inside-corner piece.

rake_a._is: the rake of the wall meeting this facet on the -Z side. Must equal that wall's own rake or a slot opens.

rake_b._is: the rake of the wall meeting this facet on the -X side.

pieces.description: A flat horizontal plate - a deck, a tier roof, a boat deck, a funnel cap. Placed on the grid at its own level and NOT derived from the walls underneath it: deriving it is what a room was, and a room made every deckhouse a shed. Because the raked walls of a tier land off-grid at the top, the deck laid over them is normally one cell larger all round, and the overhang that results is the EAVE.

gauge._is: 0.08 / 0.13 / 0.30 m. A light gauge is a visor or a hood, deck is what you walk on, heavy is a funnel cap or a bulwark capping.

pieces.description: A roof or casing top that climbs `rise` cells over its `depth`. Chains with itself: put the next one `rise` cells higher and the two are one continuous slope. This is a whaleback, a machinery-casing top, a wheelhouse visor, a companionway hood. It is NOT a wall_panel lying down - a wall's extent is vertical and a slope's is horizontal, and conflating them makes both harder to place.

The thin proud stuff, and it earns its place because without it every joint in the kit is a bare intersection of two planes, which is half of what 'blocky' means. Four profiles off one run: an eave under a deck edge, a cap over a bulwark, a coaming lip standing on a deck, a rubbing strake on a wall. Trim is where a build stops looking printed.

offset._is: pushes the run outboard in 0.25 m steps. A trim run has no height and therefore cannot carry a rake, so a strake crossing a RAKED wall is set out to meet the wall at the height it is placed - the same quarter-cell arithmetic the rake itself uses. Without this, every band on a raked wall buries itself inside the plating.

eave._is: a flat lip standing 0.30 m outboard under a deck edge

cap._is: a 0.36 m cap rail lying over a bulwark or a coaming

coaming._is: a 0.25 m lip standing up off a deck edge

strake._is: a 0.22 m band proud of a wall face
